summary: Gilir helps rain-fed farmers plan a year of crops using NASA climate history. A farmer marks their field on a globe and picks the crops they want to grow. Gilir then deterministically replays 25 years of NASA POWER daily weather and GPM IMERG rainfall for that location against FAO-56 crop water-demand profiles. It tests every valid one-year crop sequence and planting date, and returns one explained crop-rotation plan, or a specific reason why no plan fits.
details:
What it does

Gilir turns a farm location and a list of crops into a one-year crop-rotation plan, tested against 25 years of NASA weather for that exact place. It answers a question rain-fed farmers face every season: which crops, in what order, and when to plant them so they are least likely to run short of rain when they need it most.

How it works

The farmer answers four short pages:

  1. Find your farm: search a place, then outline the field on a 3D globe. Keyboard coordinate entry and a 2D fallback exist for devices without WebGL.
  2. Choose your crops from a catalogue of 40 food-crop purposes.
  3. Say where the water comes from: rain only, rain plus water when it's dry, or not sure. Every calculation uses rainfall only, so backup water changes the explanation, never the maths.
  4. Optionally sketch last year's crops on an editable timeline, and give the date the field becomes free.

The engine then:

  1. Freezes the run: inputs, crop-profile release, climate data and settings are recorded in a manifest with a hash, so any result can be reproduced and audited.
  2. Builds up to 25 replay seasons from NASA history starting on the same calendar day, and requires at least 15 complete seasons. Missing rainfall is never treated as zero and gaps are never filled.
  3. Computes daily crop water demand with the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method from NASA POWER temperature, humidity, wind, pressure and solar radiation, multiplied by FAO-56 crop coefficients for each growth stage.
  4. Compares IMERG rainfall with that demand in every rolling 7-day window of each crop's season, measuring how often rain falls short and by how much. The worst crop counts, so a wet-season crop cannot hide a dry one.
  5. Searches every valid calendar, one crop at a time, inside FAO planting windows. The search either finds candidates or proves that none fit.
  6. Ranks candidates by a fixed order: how often rainfall falls short, the average size of the shortfall, days without a planned crop, and the longest gap without a crop. The farmer's existing rotation can win, and the app then says to keep it.
  7. Returns one of six clear outcomes: a plan, a plan with warnings, not enough data, no calendar fits (with the reason), search incomplete, or a service error.

NASA data at the core

All NASA data is retrieved through the NASA POWER Daily API (v2.10.3) for the field's location, covering about 25 years of daily records:

  • NASA POWER meteorology, MERRA-2 based (T2M, T2M_MIN, T2M_MAX, RH2M, WS2M, PS): temperature, humidity, wind and pressure for FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration, which sets crop water demand.
  • NASA POWER solar radiation (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN): solar energy for the same evapotranspiration calculation.
  • GPM IMERG precipitation via POWER (IMERG_PRECTOT): daily rainfall compared against crop demand. This is the core ranking signal.
  • NASA GIBS Blue Marble Shaded Relief and Bathymetry tiles: the globe imagery on the field-picker page.

Native grids are kept and disclosed (meteorology 0.5° × 0.625°, solar 1°, IMERG 0.1°), and the app tells the farmer that drawing a field does not make NASA's grid finer. The data product, grid cell, units, conversions, content hash and retrieval time are stored with every result. No Space Agency Partner data was used.

Results on real NASA data

Six test cases were run with live NASA data, each with 25 usable seasons. The locations are illustrations, not surveyed farms.

  • Madrid, radish and barley, starting 1 March 2027: a plan with a rainfall warning. Radish 1 March to 4 April, barley 12 April to 24 August.
  • Boise, dry beans, starting 1 June 2027: a plan with a rainfall warning. Plant 1 June; the field is busy until 8 September.
  • Madrid, wheat and maize: no plan, because both planting windows cannot fit in one year. The search checked every option.
  • Boise, maize, beans and wheat: no plan, because the three crops need 426 days and a year has at most 366.
  • Bangkok beans and Ibadan maize: not enough data, because no reviewed crop profile applies there yet. Gilir declines rather than guess.

Repeat runs produce byte-identical results, and an independent FAO recomputation matched the Boise per-season numbers.

What is finished and what is next

  • The full farmer journey works on the hosted site: find the farm on a live satellite globe, choose crops, answer the water and last-year questions, and get the result. The hosted acceptance run passed all 17 checks at phone and desktop widths.
  • The results screen shows the plan as a timeline with warnings in plain words, the ranking numbers, the comparison with last year, and a details view with sources, crop assumptions and every metric per season. Each of the six outcomes has its own screen, and only real plans draw a timeline.
  • Plans are saved on the device and download as a PDF that also works offline. Reloading the page or losing the connection does not lose the plan.
  • 32 reviewed crop models are released. Crop timing is calculated from each location's own temperature history, and the result shows an estimated harvest range.

Benefits

  • Farmers get one clear, explained plan instead of guesswork, grounded in 25 years of their own location's weather.
  • Its climate data covers any point on Earth, because NASA POWER and IMERG are global, and crop coverage grows as more profiles are reviewed.
  • It is honest: when data or crop knowledge is missing, Gilir says so instead of producing a confident but wrong answer.
  • Every result can be checked: the same inputs always give the same plan, and the NASA data source of every number is recorded.

What we hope to achieve

Next we will build the results screen and deploy the full journey, add more crop profiles and temperature rules, bring in NASA SMAP soil moisture, and test the plans with farmers and agronomists. Our goal is for any rain-fed farmer, anywhere, to plan the year with evidence rather than guesswork.

Tools and languages

TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Node.js, PostgreSQL 18, Zod, MapLibre GL JS, Turf.js, pdf-lib, idb, Vitest, Playwright and Docker, hosted on Railway.

Use of AI tools

The team used AI assistants for research, writing, and help with coding, testing and documentation, including extracting crop parameters from the cited FAO publications. The team reviewed all AI-assisted output. The finished product contains no runtime AI: every plan is calculated by fixed rules.
